title: Analytical Chemistry
tagline: The wet tests that name an unknown: cations, anions and gases, each with its own unmistakable sign.

overview.intro: Analytical chemistry at this level is a memorised set of reactions that must also be understood. Every test has three parts: the reagent you add, the observation you record, and the conclusion that follows. This chapter groups the tests by what they find — metal ions, acid radicals and gases — then shows how to run them in a sensible order so that one unknown yields its identity in a handful of steps. Learn each observation as a picture: a colour, a precipitate, a smell, a flame.

facts.label: Cation tests
facts.value: Sodium hydroxide and ammonia distinguish most common metal ions by precipitate colour and solubility.

facts.label: Anion tests
facts.value: Dilute acid reveals carbonate, sulphide and sulphite; specific precipitates reveal halides and sulphate.

facts.label: Gas tests
facts.value: Each gas has a characteristic test: pop, limewater, damp litmus, smell or colour change.

facts.label: Order of testing
facts.value: Confirm anions with dilute acid first, then cations, because the reagents interfere otherwise.

learningOutcomes: Carry out and interpret the sodium hydroxide and ammonia tests for common cations, including the effect of excess reagent.
Identify acid radicals from their reactions with dilute hydrochloric acid and from their confirmatory precipitates.
Test for named gases and state the observation that identifies each one.
Write ionic equations for the precipitate-forming reactions used in the tests.
Plan a short sequence of tests that identifies both the cation and the anion in an unknown salt.

learn.title: Finding the cation with sodium hydroxide

blocks.text: Adding aqueous sodium hydroxide to a solution of a salt gives a precipitate whose colour and behaviour in excess identify the metal ion. Zinc gives a white, gelatinous precipitate that dissolves in excess to form sodium zincate, so a white precipitate that disappears points to zinc. Lead gives a white precipitate that also dissolves in excess, so a second test with potassium iodide confirms lead by giving a bright yellow precipitate of lead iodide. Copper gives a light blue precipitate that does not dissolve in excess; ammonia gives a different picture, producing a deep blue solution of the tetrammine complex. Iron(II) gives a dirty green precipitate and iron(III) a reddish brown one, and neither dissolves in excess. Ammonium salts are the exception to the rule of precipitates: they give ammonia gas instead.

items: Zn2+: white gelatinous precipitate, soluble in excess sodium hydroxide giving sodium zincate.
Pb2+: white precipitate, soluble in excess; confirms with potassium iodide giving yellow lead iodide.
Cu2+: light blue precipitate, insoluble in excess; in ammonia it forms a deep blue solution.
Fe2+: dirty green precipitate; Fe3+: reddish brown precipitate; both insoluble in excess.
NH4+: no precipitate but ammonia gas is released, identified by its smell and by damp red litmus turning blue.
Write the equation beside the colour: ZnSO4 + 2NaOH → Zn(OH)2 + Na2SO4, and in excess NaOH, Zn(OH)2 + 2NaOH → Na2ZnO2 + 2H2O, which is why the white precipitate clears.
Copper behaves differently: CuSO4 + 2NaOH → Cu(OH)2 + Na2SO4 gives the light blue solid that stays insoluble in excess alkali.

items.note: White gelatinous solid appears; adding excess alkali clears the solution as sodium zincate forms.
Reddish brown precipitate of iron(III) hydroxide stays insoluble in excess alkali.

learn.title: Ammonia, flame tests and the special cases

blocks.text: Aqueous ammonia is the second standard reagent. Added dropwise it precipitates copper hydroxide, iron(II) hydroxide and iron(III) hydroxide, and in excess it dissolves the copper precipitate to give the deep blue tetrammine complex, which is the standard confirmatory sign for copper. Added to ammonium salts together with alkali, ammonia drives off more ammonia gas, whose smell and action on damp red litmus confirm the ammonium ion. Flame tests give a third line of evidence: sodium burns golden yellow, potassium lilac (seen through blue glass to mask sodium), calcium brick red and copper green. Taken together, a precipitate colour, its behaviour in excess and a flame colour make a cation identification safe.

items: Copper plus excess ammonia gives a deep blue solution; that colour is unique among the common cations.
Ammonium salts on warming with sodium hydroxide release ammonia, which turns damp red litmus blue.
Sodium gives a golden yellow flame, potassium a lilac flame, calcium brick red and copper green.
Lead chloride dissolves in hot water and recrystallises as shiny crystals on cooling, a confirmation for lead.

items.note: A pale precipitate forms first, then dissolves in excess to give a deep blue solution.

items.text: Ammonium chloride plus sodium hydroxide on warming
items.note: Ammonia gas comes off with its characteristic pungent smell and turns damp red litmus blue.

items.meaning: Insoluble solid formed when two clear solutions are mixed, as metal hydroxides are.
More reagent added after the first result, to see whether the precipitate dissolves.
Identification of a metal ion from the colour it gives to a clean bunsen flame.

learn.title: Acid radicals: the dilute acid tests

blocks.text: The first pass at an unknown is a little dilute hydrochloric acid, because three acid radicals announce themselves by the gas they release. Carbonate fizzes with brisk effervescence and the gas turns limewater milky; sulphide gives a gas with the smell of rotten eggs that blackens lead acetate paper; sulphite gives a pungent gas that turns acidified potassium dichromate from orange to green. Once those three are excluded, the remaining anions need specific reagents. Sulphate gives a white precipitate with barium chloride that does not dissolve in dilute acid. Chloride gives a white precipitate with silver nitrate that dissolves in aqueous ammonia; bromide gives a pale yellow precipitate only partly soluble in ammonia; iodide gives a yellow precipitate soluble in potassium iodide. Nitrate is confirmed by the brown ring test or by reduction to ammonia with Devarda’s alloy.

items: Carbonate + dilute acid gives carbon dioxide; limewater turns milky and clears in excess gas.
Sulphide + dilute acid gives hydrogen sulphide; lead acetate paper turns black.
Sulphite + dilute acid gives sulphur dioxide; acidified dichromate turns from orange to green.
Sulphate + barium chloride gives white barium sulphate, insoluble in dilute hydrochloric acid.
Halides + silver nitrate give white chloride, pale yellow bromide and yellow iodide precipitates with differing ammonia solubility.

blocks.text: Gases appear in two places in this syllabus: as the products of anion tests and as the products of reactions taught elsewhere, so a single set of tests covers both. Hydrogen burns with a squeaky pop when a lit splinter is brought to it. Oxygen relights a glowing splinter, because it supports combustion vigorously. Carbon dioxide turns limewater milky. Ammonia turns damp red litmus blue and has a pungent smell. Hydrogen sulphide smells of rotten eggs and blackens lead acetate paper. Sulphur dioxide has a choking smell and bleaches damp litmus temporarily, having no colour of its own. Chlorine is pale green, has a sharp smell and bleaches damp litmus permanently because it forms hypochlorous acid. Water vapour turns white anhydrous copper sulphate blue, and steam is also seen as mist on a cool surface.

items: Hydrogen: lit splinter gives a squeaky pop; the gas burns to form water.
Oxygen: glowing splinter relights, showing strong support for combustion.
Carbon dioxide: limewater turns milky because calcium carbonate precipitates.
Ammonia: damp red litmus turns blue; the only common alkaline gas.
Chlorine and sulphur dioxide both bleach damp litmus, chlorine permanently and sulphur dioxide temporarily.

items.text: Testing the gas from zinc and dilute acid
items.note: A lit splinter at the mouth of the tube gives the characteristic squeaky pop of hydrogen.
White anhydrous copper sulphate turns blue, confirming water vapour.

items.meaning: Dilute calcium hydroxide solution used to test for carbon dioxide by turning milky.
Removal of colour; chlorine bleaches permanently while sulphur dioxide bleaches reversibly.
Confirmatory test for nitrate giving a brown ring at the junction of two layers.

learn.title: Planning an analytical scheme that actually works

blocks.text: Identification questions reward order as much as knowledge. Start with a physical inspection: colour of the solid or solution, smell if safe. Then test the anion with dilute hydrochloric acid, because those reactions are quick and the gases they give would otherwise interfere with later precipitates. Confirm any remaining acid radical with its specific reagent. Next test the cation with sodium hydroxide, noting the precipitate colour and its behaviour in excess, and confirm with ammonia, potassium iodide or a flame test as the case demands. Finally, cross-check that the proposed formula makes charge sense: a salt of Pb2+ and SO4 2- has one of each, and every observation must be consistent with that formula. Write observations before conclusions in the answer, because marks are given for what you saw.

items: Inspect first: colour, smell and state narrow the field before any reagent is used.
Anions before cations: dilute acid tests are fast and their gases would mask later results.
Always add excess reagent after the first precipitate, because solubility in excess is the distinguishing clue.
Confirm every tentative identification with a second, different test before stating a conclusion.
Balance the charge in the final formula so that the cation and anion identified actually fit together.

items.text: Unknown white salt giving hydrogen sulphide with acid
items.note: The anion is sulphide; a white precipitate with sodium hydroxide that dissolves in excess then points to zinc, giving zinc sulphide.

items.text: Unknown salt giving ammonia on warming with alkali
items.note: The cation is ammonium, so the remaining anion is found by the barium chloride or silver nitrate test.

keyPoints: Sodium hydroxide gives white zinc or lead, light blue copper, dirty green iron(II) and reddish brown iron(III) precipitates.
Zinc and lead hydroxides dissolve in excess sodium hydroxide; copper and iron hydroxides do not.
Excess aqueous ammonia dissolves copper hydroxide to give a deep blue solution.
Ammonium salts release ammonia on warming with alkali; ammonia turns damp red litmus blue.
Dilute acid identifies carbonate by brisk effervescence, sulphide by rotten-egg smell and sulphite by dichromate turning green.
Sulphate gives white barium sulphate insoluble in dilute acid; chloride, bromide and iodide give silver precipitates of differing colour and ammonia solubility.
Hydrogen pops, oxygen relights a glowing splinter, carbon dioxide milks limewater.
Chlorine bleaches permanently and sulphur dioxide temporarily, while both turn damp litmus colourless.
Anhydrous copper sulphate turning blue is the standard test for water.
Always record the observation before the conclusion, and confirm an identification with a second test.
examFocus: Table questions ask for reagent, observation and conclusion in three columns; learn them in that order.
The solubility-in-excess behaviour of a precipitate is what separates zinc and lead from copper and iron — quote it explicitly.
Gas tests must name the reagent and the sign: limewater for carbon dioxide, damp red litmus for ammonia, pop for hydrogen.
For an unknown-salt plan, state the order of testing and one reason for that order to earn the method marks.

vocabulary.meaning: Insoluble solid formed when two solutions are mixed.
Substance added to bring about a chemical test or reaction.
The negative ion of a salt, identified by its reaction with dilute acid or a specific reagent.
A second, independent test that proves the identification made by the first.
Brisk escape of gas bubbles from a liquid during a reaction.
Identification of a metal ion from the colour it produces in a flame.
Dilute calcium hydroxide used to detect carbon dioxide by turning milky.
Containing no water, as white copper sulphate before water is added.

questions.prompt: A colourless gas turned limewater milky. The gas is:
questions.explanation: Carbon dioxide precipitates calcium hydroxide as calcium carbonate, which is the milky appearance.

questions.prompt: Sodium hydroxide added to a solution gives a white precipitate that dissolves in excess. The cation is most likely:
questions.explanation: Zinc hydroxide is amphoteric and redissolves in excess alkali to give sodium zincate.

questions.prompt: The precipitate obtained with silver nitrate that dissolves readily in aqueous ammonia indicates:
questions.explanation: Silver chloride is white and dissolves in ammonia to form a soluble complex, unlike bromide or iodide.

questions.prompt: Which observation confirms the sulphite ion after dilute acid is added?
options: Acidified dichromate turns from orange to green
Limewater turns milky and stays milky
questions.answer: Acidified dichromate turns from orange to green
questions.explanation: Sulphur dioxide reduces acidified dichromate from orange to green; blackening lead acetate indicates sulphide.

questions.prompt: The gas that smells of rotten eggs and is released by sulphides with dilute acid is hydrogen __________.
questions.explanation: Hydrogen sulphide is released, and it blackens lead acetate paper as lead sulphide forms.

questions.prompt: Adding excess aqueous ammonia to a copper salt solution gives a deep blue solution of the __________ complex.
questions.explanation: Copper forms the deep blue tetraamminecopper(II) ion when excess ammonia is added.

questions.prompt: Give the reagent, observation and conclusion for the test for the sulphate ion.
questions.answer: Reagent: barium chloride solution, optionally acidified with dilute hydrochloric acid. Observation: a white precipitate forms that does not dissolve in dilute acid. Conclusion: the sulphate ion is present, since barium sulphate is insoluble in acid.
questions.explanation: Barium sulphate is the uniquely insoluble white barium salt under these conditions.

questions.prompt: How would you distinguish between iron(II) and iron(III) ions using sodium hydroxide?
questions.answer: Add sodium hydroxide solution: iron(II) gives a dirty green precipitate of iron(II) hydroxide, while iron(III) gives a reddish brown precipitate of iron(III) hydroxide; neither dissolves in excess reagent.
questions.explanation: The precipitate colour alone separates the two oxidation states of iron.

questions.prompt: State the test for ammonia gas.
questions.answer: Ammonia has a pungent smell and turns damp red litmus paper blue, because it is the only common gas that is alkaline in solution.
questions.explanation: Moisture on the paper dissolves ammonia to give hydroxide ions, which turn the litmus blue.

questions.prompt: Describe how you would confirm the chloride ion in solution, and explain why bromide and iodide are distinguished from it.
questions.answer: Add dilute nitric acid to remove interfering ions, then silver nitrate solution. Chloride gives a white precipitate of silver chloride which dissolves readily in aqueous ammonia. Bromide gives a pale yellow precipitate that is only sparingly soluble in ammonia, while iodide gives a yellow precipitate which is insoluble in ammonia but dissolves in potassium iodide to give a colourless solution. The three silver halides therefore differ in precipitate colour and in solubility behaviour, which is why the ammonia step must be carried out after the precipitate has formed.
questions.explanation: Silver chloride, bromide and iodide differ in lattice energy, so their colours and ammonia solubilities follow a regular pattern.

questions.prompt: A white salt gives brisk effervescence with dilute hydrochloric acid, and the gas turns limewater milky. Name the anion, write the ionic equation for the gas with limewater, and give one use of the salt.
questions.answer: The anion is carbonate. Carbon dioxide is evolved, and with limewater it forms insoluble calcium carbonate: Ca2+ + 2OH- + CO2 → CaCO3 + H2O. The salt is therefore a carbonate such as sodium carbonate, which is used in glass making and as a washing soda for removing grease.
questions.explanation: Brisk effervescence with dilute acid plus a milky limewater test is the standard carbonate identification.

questions.prompt: An unknown salt is colourless and gives a yellow precipitate with potassium iodide. On adding sodium hydroxide it gives a white precipitate that dissolves in excess. Identify the cation and anion, and justify each test.
questions.answer: The yellow precipitate with potassium iodide is lead(II) iodide, so lead ions are present. The white precipitate with sodium hydroxide that dissolves in excess is lead(II) hydroxide, which is amphoteric and forms plumbite in excess alkali; this independently confirms lead. The cation is therefore Pb2+. Because the salt is colourless and no anion test result is given, the anion must be established separately, most commonly by the absence of carbonate effervescence and the behaviour of the barium chloride test; the cation identification itself rests on two consistent lead-specific reactions.
questions.explanation: Two independent lead-specific signs — yellow PbI2 and amphoteric Pb(OH)2 — make the cation identification reliable.
